title: Hypoglycaemia in Adults
clinicalScenario: Outline only. Planned scope: Conscious and unconscious patient pathways, treatment, recheck, causes (insulin, sulfonylurea, non-diabetic), safe discharge criteria. Candidate sources to verify: JBDS-IP hospital management of hypoglycaemia; ADA Standards of Care.

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult (over 18 years) Emergency Department (ED) and inpatient treatment of hypoglycaemia in people with diabetes, based on the Joint British Diabetes Societies (JBDS) 2023 guideline and the Saudi Ministry of Health (MOH) inpatient hypoglycaemia protocol. Neonatal, paediatric and non-diabetic hypoglycaemia work-up are outside this protocol.
findings: Full protocol rebuilt from the source dossier opened on 2026-10-21; exact source locations are recorded in each investigation and medicine row.
The original outline remains preserved; this additive version is non-current and pending clinical review.
unverifiedSections: Normal reference ranges are typical adult values, not taken from the cited guidelines.
Symptoms, signs, precipitants, differentials and pathophysiology are standard clinical content and were not extracted line by line from the sources.
JBDS page numbers were inferred from an automated reading of the PDF; the Saudi MOH protocol has no page numbers, so section headings are cited. Check both before clinical sign-off.
The Saudi MOH protocol has no stated publication date, and its relationship to the Saudi Diabetes Clinical Practice Guidelines (pp. 69–70) was not reconciled.
Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) registration and availability of glucagon and glucose products were not checked.
JBDS does not define mild, moderate or severe by mmol/L; the Saudi 2.5 mmol/L split applies only to the 50% dextrose branch.

JBDS Appendix 5 (IV glucose infusion details), glucagon reconstitution steps and thiamine for alcohol-related hypoglycaemia were not in the opened text; follow the product leaflet for glucagon preparation.

Renal, hepatic and age adjustments for the drugs added in this revision are from manufacturer labels (UK Summary of Product Characteristics, US prescribing information and a New Zealand data sheet), not from Saudi Food and Drug Authority labels.

pathophysiology.summary: Hypoglycaemia in diabetes is usually caused by treatment that lowers glucose faster than intake or hepatic glucose output can match.
keyMechanisms: Insulin and sulfonylureas are the usual causes; their effect can last 24–36 hours, longer with renal impairment.
Missed or delayed meals, extra exercise, alcohol, renal or liver failure and dosing errors are common triggers.
Low glucose reduces glucose supply to the brain, causing confusion, reduced consciousness and seizures; adrenaline release causes sweating and tremor.

symptoms: Confusion, odd behaviour, drowsiness, visual disturbance, headache.
physicalSigns: Reduced consciousness, seizure, focal neurological signs that resolve with glucose.
redFlags: Unable to swallow safely or unconscious.
Capillary blood glucose still below 4.0 mmol/L after 3 treatment cycles or 30–45 minutes.
Sulfonylurea or long-acting insulin overdose, or renal impairment (prolonged effect).
Seizure or persistent confusion after glucose is corrected.
precipitants: Insulin or sulfonylurea dose too high, missed meal, extra exercise, alcohol, acute kidney injury, liver failure, sepsis.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Focal deficit that does not resolve when glucose is normal
Normal capillary glucose, smell of alcohol
Fever, raised inflammatory markers; hypoglycaemia may coexist

ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Treat immediately; recheck 10–15 minutes after oral treatment, up to 3 treatments

clinicalManagement.title: Immediate
actions: Confirm capillary glucose below 4.0 mmol/L and check airway, breathing, circulation and consciousness.
Stop any insulin infusion immediately; restart it once the episode is treated and review the dose.
Conscious and able to swallow: give oral rapid-acting carbohydrate.
Unable to swallow safely: give glucose gel, IV glucose or glucagon according to access and glycogen stores.
Recheck capillary glucose 10–15 minutes after oral treatment (5 minutes after IV dextrose in the Saudi MOH protocol).

clinicalManagement.title: Ongoing
actions: Repeat treatment if glucose is still below 4.0 mmol/L, up to 3 times; call for medical help if still low after 30–45 minutes or 3 cycles.
Once glucose is above 4.0 mmol/L and the patient has recovered, give long-acting carbohydrate.
Do not omit a due insulin injection; review which dose was active.

clinicalManagement.title: Escalation
actions: Still below 4.0 mmol/L after 3 cycles: medical review and IV glucose.
Sulfonylurea or long-acting insulin effect: monitor glucose for at least 24–48 hours.

clinicalManagement.title: Disposition
actions: Admit for prolonged monitoring if sulfonylurea or long-acting insulin was the cause, in renal impairment, or after severe hypoglycaemia needing IV treatment.

learningObjectives: Recognise hypoglycaemia and choose oral, IV or glucagon treatment safely.
Know the recheck timing and follow-on carbohydrate.
Know why sulfonylurea and long-acting insulin need prolonged monitoring.
pitfalls: Stopping an insulin infusion but forgetting to restart it.
Treating hyperglycaemic rebound with stat insulin.
keyPoints: Use IV glucose when access exists and glycogen stores may be depleted.
Continue glucose monitoring for 24–48 hours after long-acting causes.
